clue.text: An attitude I assume as ruler of the waves

parts.note: a pose is an attitude struck, a posture adopted
to don is to put on or assume, as clothing or a manner

explanation.surface: Someone strikes a lordly pose, as if commanding the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as' is only a link between wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek god of the sea is the classical master of the oceans.

clue.text: When speaking, choose to cut a meal

indicators.note: When speaking says the words are to be heard rather than read

parts.note: to pick is to choose; a nick is a small cut

explanation.surface: Someone, while talking, opts to skip lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' is a link between the two sounded words.
explanation.definitionFit: An outdoor meal eaten from a hamper is a type of lunch out in the open.

clue.text: One's up quite a long way in comparison

indicators.note: up in a down clue means the word is written upwards, reversed

parts.note: one's is short for one is, I'S
a mile is quite a long distance

explanation.surface: A traveller notes how far they have climbed by comparing distances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A figure of speech likening one thing to another with 'like' or 'as' is a comparison.

clue.text: Embarrassed: I will get a comb

parts.note: to tease hair is to comb it to raise it

explanation.surface: Someone is mortified at having to be seen with a comb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling awkward and uncomfortable in company is being self-conscious.

clue.text: Escaped prisoners are not agreeing …

explanation.surface: Runaway convicts are at odds with each other.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on to 6-down's clue, but this clue is complete in itself. Escaped prisoners are no longer in custody.
explanation.definitionFit: Prisoners on the run are no longer held in custody; the idiom also means incongruous, inappropriate.

clue.text: There's talk when creature goes round, round, round ship

indicators.note: the second round means the turned animal wraps itself around what follows
goes round tells us the creature's name is turned back to front

parts.note: a pig is a farmyard creature
a round shape looks like the letter O
SS is the abbreviation for steamship

explanation.surface: Chatter breaks out as some animal circles a vessel again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: Three 'round's do three jobs: 'goes round' reverses PIG to GIP, the second 'round' puts GIP around the rest, the third is O. 'There's' and 'when' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Idle chatter about other people is the noun's everyday sense, as in office tittle-tattle.

clue.text: … to holding vicar up in full view

indicators.note: up in a down clue tells us the whole construction is written upwards
holding means the word to contains the clergyman

parts.note: taken as written
Rev, reverend, is a vicar's title

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue, a clergyman is lifted up for all to see.
explanation.walkthrough: TO holding REV gives TREVO, which 'up' reverses. The leading ellipsis just links the surface to 4-down.
explanation.definitionFit: Something open and not concealed is plainly visible to all.

clue.text: Sibyl keeps at a distance from Jack

indicators.note: keeps means the prophetess word holds the distance word inside

parts.note: a sibyl is a prophetess, a seer
afar means at a distance

explanation.surface: A prophetess keeps away from a man called Jack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack' looks like a name, but a jack or jack tar is a sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: Jack tar is old slang for a sailor, a man who goes to sea.

clue.text: Characteristic article on the stage

explanation.surface: A typical item used in a theatre production.
explanation.definitionFit: A quality or trait of something; also a stage prop, an object used by actors.

clue.text: Without money, rival is finished

indicators.note: Without in its old sense of outside means the rival word goes around the money

parts.note: to rival someone is to compete with them
L stands for pound (libra), a unit of money

explanation.surface: A competitor who has run out of cash is done for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking' but means 'outside', putting COMPETE around L.
explanation.definitionFit: Something whole and done is entire, with nothing left to do.

clue.text: Load put back into river boat

indicators.note: into means the reversed word goes inside the river

parts.note: the Po is the great river of northern Italy

indicators.note: put back signals that the word for load is written in reverse

parts.note: to lade is to load a ship or cart

explanation.surface: Cargo is reloaded onto a riverboat.
explanation.walkthrough: LADE reversed gives EDAL, which goes into PO.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedal-powered pleasure craft hired at seaside resorts and lakes is a small boat.

clue.text: Lead sounds like the first element to float

indicators.note: sounds like tells us the words are to be heard, not spelt

parts.note: principal means first, and a buoy is a thing that floats

explanation.surface: A chemist claims a lead-like element was the first to float.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' is not the metal but the leading role in a British pantomime, traditionally played by a young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: In pantomime the hero, the starring role, is played by an actress in breeches.

clue.text: Expanse of water, one quarter rented

parts.note: the Roman numeral I is one
N, north, is one of the four compass quarters
let means rented out, as a flat is let

explanation.surface: An estate agent describes a lakeside property, a quarter of it already leased.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrow arm of sea running into the land is a stretch of water.

clue.text: He could become a fit master

indicators.note: could become says the letters of the following words turn into something new

explanation.surface: An unfit man could, with training, become a fit master.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He' is the definition: a ship's officer second to the captain, who might one day rise to master. The anagram of A FIT MASTER gives the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: The officer next below the captain of a merchant vessel is a man who could one day command.

clue.text: Tunnel diggers have to stay solvent

explanation.surface: Workers boring from both sides must also keep within budget.
explanation.walkthrough: Tunnellers working from both sides need their two headings to join up in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Tunnel teams must join their two halves; financially, the idiom means living within one's income.

clue.text: Subscription certain to cover one source of annoyance

indicators.note: to cover means the certain word goes around the other pieces

parts.note: sure means certain
the Roman numeral I is one
a gnat is a small biting fly, a source of annoyance

explanation.surface: Someone is sure that paying for a magazine will bring irritation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Subscription' is used in its old sense of a name written at the foot of a document.
explanation.definitionFit: To subscribe originally meant to write one's name beneath, so a subscription is a name signed underneath.

clue.text: Shaky alibi outlined by J.R. — at the start of Dallas he's in prison

indicators.note: outlined by means the initials J.R. form an outline around the rest

parts.note: the initials J and R, as in the Dallas character

indicators.note: Shaky means the letters of the word alibi are unsteady and rearranged
at the start of picks the first letter of the following word

explanation.surface: J.R. Ewing of the TV soap Dallas has a weak alibi and ends up behind bars.
explanation.walkthrough: J.R. Ewing was the scheming oil baron of the US TV soap Dallas; 'Shaky' scrambles the alibi, which sits between his initials.
explanation.definitionFit: A convict, an old lag, is someone serving time.

clue.text: Show of force from rock-climbing bear

indicators.note: climbing in a down clue means the rock word is written upwards

parts.note: the Rock is Gibraltar, short form Gib
to stick is to bear or tolerate, as in 'can't stick it'

explanation.surface: A bear clambering up a cliff makes a show of strength.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rock-climbing' reads as one sport, but GIB (Gibraltar, the Rock) climbs to BIG.
explanation.definitionFit: Big-stick diplomacy means the threat of military power to back up negotiation.

clue.text: Snake swallows insects, and goes round the town down under

indicators.note: swallows means the snake takes the insects inside it

parts.note: an asp is a venomous snake
lice are small parasitic insects
rings means encircles, goes round

explanation.surface: A snake eats bugs and slithers round an Australian outback town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'down under' is everyday slang for Australia; the town is in the Northern Territory. 'and' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A well-known settlement in the middle of the Australian outback is a town there.

clue.text: Go right

explanation.surface: A two-word instruction to turn the other way.
explanation.definitionFit: To repair to a place is to go there; to repair is to fix or put right.

clue.text: Stick notice on present

parts.note: an ad is a notice, an advertisement
here means present, as in a roll call

explanation.surface: Glue a poster onto a gift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To cling fast or be glued is to stay attached.

clue.text: American boards wrecked Italian liner

indicators.note: boards means gets on, so the American goes inside the rest
wrecked shows the letters of the word Italian are smashed up and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A US passenger climbs aboard a shipwrecked Italian vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrecked' scrambles the Italian, and 'boards' puts the American aboard, as a passenger boards a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cunard ship torpedoed in 1915 was a famous ocean liner.

clue.text: Act it out without words

indicators.note: out signals the letters of the words act it are disordered

explanation.surface: A mime artist is told to perform silently.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacit agreement is understood or implied without being spoken.

clue.text: A loaf in the van

parts.note: loaf is slang for head, as in 'use your loaf'

explanation.surface: Bread is carried in a delivery van.
explanation.walkthrough: 'van' is the vanguard, the front, not a vehicle; 'loaf' is British slang for head, from rhyming slang loaf of bread.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in the vanguard means being at the front, leading the way.

clue.text: I would take love in a cold climate to be madness!

parts.note: I'd is short for I would

indicators.note: in means the love letter goes inside the cold word

parts.note: a cold climate is an icy one
love is nil in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone thinks romance in a freezing country would be sheer folly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take' is a link; 'in' sets love inside the cold climate, after I'd.
explanation.definitionFit: Utter foolishness or stupidity is a kind of madness.

clue.text: A redoubt is constructed to be unshakeable

indicators.note: is constructed means the letters are built up again in a new order

explanation.surface: A fortification is built so as to be impregnable.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone stubborn and immovable cannot be swayed.

clue.text: Information about return of satisfactory plane

indicators.note: about means the information word goes around the reversed piece

parts.note: data is information

indicators.note: return of means the word for satisfactory is turned back

parts.note: OK means satisfactory

explanation.surface: Records show an acceptable aircraft coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return of' turns satisfactory backwards, and 'about' wraps the information around it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Douglas DC-3 was known in RAF service as a twin-engined transport aircraft of this name.

clue.text: My plane is often: flown thus

explanation.surface: A pilot exclaims about how aircraft are usually flown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'George' is airmen's slang for the automatic pilot, so a plane is often flown by it.
explanation.definitionFit: An old exclamation of surprise like 'goodness'; aviators nicknamed the autopilot George.
